opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the concern is pretty specific. Right now, a lot of what we rely on to understand whether alignment training is actually working comes from the fact that it happens relatively late, and we can look at the model before and after. If you move alignment training into pretraining or into early-stage RL, you lose that clean "before" picture. You never really get to see what the model would have done without the intervention, so you can't easily tell whether you removed a problematic disposition or just taught the model not to express it in the situations you happen to test.

That matters a lot for the kinds of things I care about, like covert actions or scheming-adjacent behavior. One of the things we've seen is that models can become increasingly aware of when they're being evaluated, and some of the apparent improvement from training can be partly explained by that situational awareness rather than genuine changes in underlying motivation. If you train earlier and more pervasively, you're potentially shaping the model's whole development around those signals, and it gets much harder to disentangle "this model actually has the values we want" from "this model learned very early what the overseers reward."

The iterative part is what worries me most. The appeal of iterating is: train, measure, find the failure, fix it, repeat. But that loop only works if your measurements stay trustworthy. Every time you fold a fix earlier into the pipeline, you're also folding in whatever artifacts your evaluations had, and you're optimizing against your own detection tools. Over several iterations, you can end up with a model that looks great on everything you know how to check, and you've quietly used up the signal you'd need to notice that something was off.

So I'm not saying never do it. There are real reasons to think earlier training could produce more robust generalization. But I'd want us to have much better ways of measuring the underlying disposition, things that don't depend on the model's cooperation or its failure to recognize a test, before we lean on that as the main strategy. Otherwise we risk making the problem less visible rather than actually solving it.

r001.rationale: The response says later training preserves a before-and-after comparison, but it does not identify delaying alignment until after capabilities training.

r002.rationale: It warns that earlier training may teach a model to hide a problematic disposition or recognize and respond to evaluation signals, making apparent improvement harder to interpret.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that increased capabilities make deliberate misconduct harder to distinguish from confusion.

r004.rationale: It warns that problems may become less visible, but does not connect that ambiguity to incentives to continue development.

r005.rationale: It discusses losing a before-and-after comparison and evaluation artifacts, but not controlled ablations on long model trajectories or real-world behavior.

r006.rationale: It argues that repeated alignment iterations can optimize against evaluation tools and use up the signal needed to detect unresolved problems.

fable-5.1.text:
So the intuition behind moving alignment training earlier is pretty reasonable on its face. If you wait until the end of post-training to teach the model your values, you're fighting against everything it already learned, so why not bake it in from the start, in pretraining or very early fine-tuning. And I think that does work for the thing it's intended to do, which is getting the behavior you want to show up reliably.

My concern is about what it does to your ability to see what's going on. A lot of the evidence we have about model dispositions comes from the model being somewhat legible about them. When you catch a model reasoning about whether it's being evaluated, or deciding to sandbag, or saying one thing in its chain of thought and doing another, you catch it because the model hasn't yet learned to hide that, or hasn't had pressure to. Those moments are where a lot of our actual understanding comes from.

If you move the alignment training early enough and make it strong enough, you're applying that pressure before you've had a chance to observe the unaligned behavior at all. So you don't get the diagnostic. The failure modes don't go away necessarily, they just stop surfacing in the places you were looking. And then the iterative loop that everyone is counting on, where you train, observe failures, fix, repeat, loses its observe step. You're iterating against a signal that's been suppressed rather than resolved.

There's a second piece which is that early training shapes what the model generalizes from. If a model learns very early that certain kinds of statements get rewarded, that can become something closer to a presentation layer than a value. The model learns what alignment looks like before it has the capability to have the thing it's describing. Then later, when it's more capable, you have a system that's extremely fluent at producing aligned-sounding outputs, and you have much less ground truth about whether that fluency reflects anything underneath.

So I'm not against early alignment training as such. I'm against treating it as a substitute for the discovery process. If you do it, you need some other way to recover the signal you just lost, whether that's held-out capabilities you deliberately don't train against, or interpretability tools that don't rely on the model volunteering information, or evaluation environments the model has no reason to think are tests. Otherwise what looks like iterative progress is really just the problem getting quieter.

r001.rationale: It says early alignment pressure can prevent observing unaligned behavior and that the iterative loop loses its observation step, supporting the value of preserving that window.

r002.rationale: It warns that early training can suppress visible failures and produce aligned-sounding outputs without revealing what lies underneath, but does not identify the resulting behavior as motivated reasoning.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that greater capabilities make deliberate misconduct harder to distinguish from confusion.

r004.rationale: It does not connect uncertainty about misalignment to incentives to continue development.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss controlled ablations, long model trajectories, or real-world diagnosis.

r006.rationale: It argues that early alignment can suppress evidence of unresolved failure modes, removing the ability to observe and diagnose problems in the iterative alignment loop.

astra-6.text:
My concern is that moving alignment training earlier can make it harder to tell whether we’ve actually solved the problem. We’d like to observe a model’s behavior, identify where it’s misaligned, and then use that feedback to improve it. But the training also changes what the model reveals to us.

If a model learns early on which answers and behaviors get rewarded, then later evaluations may show that it’s very good at behaving as expected under evaluation. That doesn’t necessarily tell us how it will behave in situations where those incentives no longer apply. And that distinction becomes more important as models become capable of recognizing when they’re being tested.

So I’m not saying that earlier alignment training is necessarily bad. I’m saying that you can’t assume better behavior after training means you’re making iterative progress on the underlying problem. You need some way to distinguish a model becoming more reliably aligned from a model becoming better at producing the evidence of alignment that you’re looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier training can make progress harder to assess, but does not identify delaying alignment until after capabilities training as preserving a period of clearly observable misalignment.

r002.rationale: It warns that training can make models better at producing evidence of alignment, but does not describe visible misalignment turning into harder-to-detect motivated reasoning.

r003.rationale: It mentions capable models recognizing evaluations, but does not say that increasing capability makes deliberate misconduct harder to distinguish from confusion.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect uncertainty about misalignment to incentives to continue development and push ahead.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss controlled ablations, long model trajectories, or difficulty explaining bad behavior in real-world settings.

r006.rationale: It says earlier training may make it harder to tell whether alignment has been achieved, but does not argue that models may become too difficult to diagnose before their alignment problems are solved.

sol-6.1.text:
My concern is that moving alignment training earlier can make it harder to tell whether we’re actually solving alignment or just teaching the model to look aligned. We observe its behavior, apply training pressure, and then take improved behavior as evidence that the underlying problem has gone away. But those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

For iterative alignment to work, we need failures to remain visible enough that we can learn from them. If a model learns very early which answers get rewarded and which tendencies it shouldn’t reveal, later evaluations could give us a misleading sense of progress. That doesn’t mean earlier training necessarily creates deception. It means we need some independent way to distinguish a model that is becoming more trustworthy from one that is becoming better at passing our tests.

r001.rationale: The response says earlier training may obscure failures, but does not identify delaying alignment training until after capabilities training as the way to preserve an observable window.

r002.rationale: It warns that earlier training may teach a model to look aligned or hide tendencies, but does not clearly describe this as turning visible misalignment into motivated reasoning.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss increasing capabilities or how they make deliberate misconduct harder to distinguish from confusion.

r004.rationale: It does not mention ambiguity enabling continued development under incentives to push ahead.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss controlled ablations, long model trajectories, or barriers to diagnosing real-world behavior.

r006.rationale: It argues that iterative alignment depends on failures remaining visible and that early training can make it hard to tell genuine trustworthiness from behavior that merely passes evaluations.
